questions.q: In this capstone's diagnostic sequence, what is checked first when a ticket says a VM can't be reached?
options: Whether the VM is actually running, to rule out the simplest explanation before investigating networking or the OS
The contents of /var/log/auth.log on the VM
Whether the SSH client on the admin's own laptop is up to date
The VM's billing status in the Azure portal
questions.explain: Confirming the VM's power state is the fastest, broadest check, and it's done before anything narrower.

questions.q: What was the actual root cause of the connectivity problem in this scenario?
options: The NSG's inbound SSH rule still allowed only the company's old office IP range, which no longer matched after an office move
The VM's operating system had crashed and needed a full reinstall
The route table was missing a default route to the internet entirely
The SSH key pair had expired and needed to be regenerated
questions.explain: The rule itself never changed — the office's outbound IP range did, so legitimate traffic stopped matching the allow rule.

questions.q: Why does checking the route table matter in this diagnosis, even though it turns out not to be the problem?
options: It rules out a bad user-defined route overriding the default internet path, narrowing down where the real problem must be
Checking it is required by Azure before any NSG rule can be viewed
It automatically repairs any NSG misconfiguration it finds
Route tables cannot be checked once a VM has booted
questions.explain: Even a check that comes back clean is useful — it eliminates one more layer as the source of the problem.

questions.q: Why is an essentially empty /var/log/auth.log treated as meaningful evidence, rather than as 'nothing to see here'?
options: No attempts at all means the traffic never reached the VM, which points at the network/NSG layer rather than at sshd or authentication
An empty log file always means the VM has never been turned on
Auth.log only records successful logins, never failed ones, so it can't be used for diagnosis
The log being empty means sshd itself is not installed
questions.explain: If authentication had actually been attempted and failed, the log would show it; showing nothing means the request never arrived.

questions.q: This lesson describes a layered checking order: network, then cloud configuration, then OS/services. Why check in that order rather than the reverse?
options: It moves from the broadest, fastest checks to the narrowest ones, so you don't start changing the wrong thing first
Operating system checks are always faster than network checks, so they should be eliminated last for efficiency
Cloud providers require NSG checks to happen only after OS checks are complete
The order doesn't actually matter — any sequence reaches the same diagnosis equally fast
questions.explain: Starting broad and narrowing down avoids wasting time changing OS-level settings when the real problem sits one layer out.
